manuscript_title: Intrafilament nucleotide exchange in a prokaryotic actin homolog

required_revisions.text: Remove or replace the in-preparation citation at line 282 ('We observed similar effects for E136A and D158A of G. stearothermophilus MreB (De San Eustaquio-Campillo et al., in preparation)'). Either present the underlying data in this manuscript (main or supplementary figure with methods and n), or delete the claim. An unpublished, unresolvable source cannot carry a mechanistic claim in a published record.

Release the Monte Carlo model in full: deposit code with a resolvable DOI and state in the Methods the reaction scheme, rate laws, initial/boundary conditions, stochastic algorithm and time step, number of simulation runs and whether plotted traces are single runs or averages, random seed(s) or a seed-averaging statement, and the parameter-fitting procedure. Add the promised one-way sensitivity analysis (k_hyd, k-,d, k+,n, k-,n varied 2–10 fold) and a quantitative goodness-of-fit metric for simulated vs. observed disassembly (Fig. 4C, S10). State explicitly how many of the ~11 parameters were fitted versus constrained by independent measurement.

Deposit all raw data (HS-AFM, TIRF, anisotropy, ATPase replicates, in vivo imaging) on Zenodo with a resolvable DOI and cite the accession in the Data Availability statement. Replace 'available from the corresponding authors upon request' and 'will be deposited after publication' with a live identifier. Also deposit the custom MATLAB extraction/rate-fitting script.

Revise the novelty framing as the authors propose: change the line-268 'first report of nucleotide cycling within a biological polymer' to a claim restricted to exchange along an intact filament lattice, explicitly contrasted with end-localized exchange in ParM (ref. 29), and add the promised Discussion paragraph making that contrast.

In the Results and Discussion, state explicitly that transient subunit dissociation with lateral membrane diffusion and rebinding is an alternative account of the ATP* FRAP recovery, and lay out the argument given in the rebuttal (TFLime vs. ATP* recovery dissociation; segment-localized fragmentation in the capping experiment) as evidence favouring intrafilament exchange without claiming it is dispositive. Name position-resolved FRAP as the decisive future test. If position-resolved FRAP is not added, the mechanism must be presented as the favoured interpretation rather than an established result, including in the abstract.

Report absolute Pi release rates (Pi/min/MreB) for WT, E136A and D158A in Fig. 3A and the text, replacing the qualitative 'markedly reduced', and compare the residual rate to the measured polymerization rate (subunits/min) so readers can judge whether residual hydrolysis could be mechanistically sufficient.

Add complete FRAP quantification for Fig. 3E and 3F: bleach radius, recovery half-time, mobile fraction, and n filaments per condition, plus the apparent exchange rate computed for comparison with the fitted k-,n = 0.0141 s-1.

Add a Methods subsection specifying all TSOAX/SOAX parameter values (thresholds, window size, sensitivity, ridge/stretch settings) per dataset, and the criteria used for the 'visual inspection' selection of the linear fitting window for elongation rates.

For every group comparison, name the specific test used, report the normality/assumptions check outcome, and give exact p-values — in particular for Fig. 3D and Fig. 4B, where only n is currently given.

State sample sizes and number of independent biological replicates for all experiments currently shown as representative only: the CCCP delocalization experiment (Fig. 4J, number of cells and replicates), the FRAP experiments (Fig. 3E, 3F) and the capping experiment (Fig. 4G–H).

Correct or clarify the flagged citation attributions: (a) verify the species simulated in ref. 18 and correct the 'Escherichia coli MreB filaments recruit CL' statement at line 118; (b) at line 19, separate the crystallographic source from the MD source rather than attributing both to Colavin et al. 2014; (c) at line 9, clarify whether van den Ent et al. 2014 studied MreB in solution and whether the membrane-surface statement is an extension; (d) at line 29, confirm that Garner et al. 2004 reports the equivalent ParM E136A ATPase phenotype directly, or mark it as inference from structural homology; (e) cite a foundational actin reference for nucleotide trapping at line 8 alongside ref. 8.

Clarify the publication status and dates of refs. 17 (Adriaans et al., Biophys. J., dated 2026, DOI 10.1016/j.bpj.2026.06.003) and 18 (Baileeves et al., 2025). If ref. 17 is in press by the same first author, label it as such and flag the self-citation; because the protein purification and ATPase protocols cite it as provenance, confirm in the Methods that the versions given here are self-contained (the audit indicates they largely are).

Add the clarification the authors propose regarding the ~1000-fold discrepancy between the elongation-derived Cc (~0.003 uM) and prior solution estimates (1–2 uM), stating explicitly that the two values report different rate-limiting steps (membrane-templated elongation vs. solution nucleation) and are not directly comparable.

Soften the 'partially unfolded' interpretation of nucleotide-free MreB to a hypothesis consistent with, but not demonstrated by, the kinetics, and add the corresponding limitation to the Discussion. If CD/SEC data are added, report them with full methods; if not, the hedged wording stands.

Hedge the in vivo ATP-locked interpretation of the E136A CCCP experiment to acknowledge that altered nucleotide affinity is not fully excluded as a contributor, incorporating the rebuttal's D158A/ADP-flush argument into the text. If the D158A CCCP control is performed, report it with n and replicates.

Ensure all supplementary materials referenced (Supplementary Text on modeling, Figs. S1–S11, Tables S1–S4 including primer and plasmid sequences and lipid compositions, Movies 1–9) are posted with the preprint and reachable, since primer sequences, plasmid sequences and the model description are currently only promised there.

minor_suggestions: Add software version numbers for ImageJ/FIJI, SOAX, TSOAX, MATLAB and PRISM (Omnipose, Igor Pro, Kintek Explorer and SP2000 versions are already given).
Provide catalogue numbers for the nucleotides and the ATTO-488 nucleotide analogues (Jena Biosciences), and the vendor for phosphatidylglycerol used in Fig. 1E–F.
State whether E136A, D158A and the pFAST fusion constructs and B. subtilis strains were sequence-verified, and give the parental genetic background of the RCL strains.

Spot-check the numerical entries in Table 1 against their primary sources (refs. 8, 25, 35, 36, 40–47) and indicate in the legend which values are direct quotations, which are recalculated, and the error convention for entries currently lacking one.
Standardise error-bar definitions across all figure legends (SD, SEM or CI), including Fig. 4E–F where bars are shown on one side only.
Specify the CCCP vehicle/solvent and its final concentration, and whether a vehicle-only control was imaged.
Consider a brief statement of how many independent HS-AFM sessions and cantilevers contributed to the n=7 elongation-rate measurements, since tip geometry is fabricated per-cantilever.

weaknesses.text: The central claim that 'nucleotide exchange within filaments tunes their stability' rests on the ADP-induced depolymerization experiment (Fig. 4A–C), but an alternative explanation is not excluded: rapid ADP loading could simply reflect a change in nucleotide affinity under the new buffer conditions rather than exchange occurring within intact filaments. The FRAP experiment with ATP* (Fig. 3F) shows recovery, but recovery of a fluorescent nucleotide analog does not prove that the same exchange mechanism operates under physiological ATP/ADP ratios or that it is the primary stability-tuning mechanism in vivo. The capping experiment (Fig. 4G–H) is suggestive but involves E136A (an ATPase mutant), not WT filaments, so it does not directly test whether intrafilament exchange in WT filaments is necessary for the observed ADP-induced destabilization. A direct measurement of nucleotide composition within filaments (e.g., by mass spectrometry or NMR) would definitively establish that exchange occurs and quantify its rate relative to hydrolysis.

The critical concentration (Cc) is reported as 0.003 µM (Table 1, Fig. 2E), but the text states 'At 0.05 µM MreB, isolated short filaments appeared within one minute' (line 147–148), which is 17-fold above Cc; this makes it unclear whether the plateau in elongation rate (Fig. 2E) reflects a genuine saturation of membrane-binding sites or a concentration-dependent artifact of the experimental setup, and the authors do not discuss whether the Cc value is reliable given the membrane-templated polymerization mechanism.

The statement 'nucleotide exchange within MreB filaments defines a new class of biological polymer behavior' (Abstract, line 8–9) is presented as a novel finding, but the manuscript does not explicitly compare the rate or mechanism of intrafilament exchange in MreB to any other polymer system (actin, tubulin, ParM) to justify the claim of novelty; the comparison to actin is qualitative ('no evidence of rapid nucleotide exchange') rather than quantitative.

questions: Figure 3F (FRAP with ATP*): what is the half-time of recovery and the mobile fraction, and how do these compare to the rate of intrafilament nucleotide exchange predicted by the model (kex = 0.014 s⁻¹)?

In the Monte Carlo model (Fig. 4D, Supplementary Information), what is the sensitivity of the predicted filament stability to the assumed rate of intrafilament nucleotide exchange (k+,n and k−,n)—i.e., if exchange were 10-fold slower or faster, would the model still fit the experimental data?

The authors state that 'MreB, which was purified in a nucleotide-free state, is partially unfolded in the absence of nucleotide' (line 103–104) as an explanation for slow ATP binding kinetics; is there direct evidence (e.g., circular dichroism, size-exclusion chromatography) that nucleotide-free MreB is indeed partially unfolded?

weaknesses.text: **Mechanism of filament stability conflation**: The authors propose that intrafilament nucleotide exchange tunes filament stability, but the evidence does not cleanly separate this from end-capping by ATP/ADP-Pi-bound subunits. In Fig. 4, WT filaments disassemble slowly after buffer wash (−1.03 ± 0.54 nm·s⁻¹) and rapidly when ADP is added (−70.34 ± 29.89 nm·s⁻¹). The model predicts both behaviors by invoking nucleotide exchange, but an alternative explanation is that end-capping by ATP-bound subunits (present initially) stabilizes filaments, and exchange merely reflects the kinetic consequence of losing that cap. The capping experiment (Fig. 4G–H) attempts to address this by showing that E136A-capped WT filaments still fragment in ADP, but this does not isolate the contribution of intrafilament exchange to stability in the WT case. The authors state "filament ends are capped by one or several ATP or ADP-Pi-bound subunits" (line 331–332) but do not quantify cap size, lifetime, or the relative contribution of capping vs. exchange to the observed disassembly kinetics. This ambiguity undermines the claim that exchange is a primary tuning mechanism rather than a secondary consequence of nucleotide dynamics.

HS-AFM elongation rate (14.4 ± 10.16 nm·s⁻¹, n=7) is derived from filament segments with "transient immobilization or reduced mobility, likely due to transient interactions with the AFM tip" (lines 160–162). This non-random sampling introduces bias: immobilized segments may elongate differently than freely diffusing ones, and the small n and high SD (70% of the mean) make this a weak anchor for the plateau interpretation in TIRF. The authors acknowledge tracking difficulties but do not quantify the bias or sensitivity of the conclusion to this estimate.

FRAP experiments (Fig. 3E–F) use different interpretations for the same phenomenon: TFLime shows no recovery (attributed to photochemical trapping), while ATP* shows rapid recovery (attributed to nucleotide exchange). The claim that TFLime trapping is irreversible is not independently validated; if TFLime can exchange under some conditions, the absence of recovery in Fig. 3E does not prove monomers are immobile. The authors should either measure TFLime exchange kinetics independently or use ATP* alone to quantify monomer turnover.

Nucleotide binding kinetics (Table 1, Fig. 1D) are measured on soluble monomers, but polymerization occurs on membranes where local concentration, lipid interactions, and conformational constraints differ. The relevance of the measured Kd values (ATP: 0.50 µM, ADP: 0.56 µM) to the filament state is assumed but not validated; a direct measurement of nucleotide affinity in membrane-bound filaments would strengthen the model.

The critical concentration (Cₜ ≈ 0.003 µM) is derived from a linear fit at low MreB concentrations (0.01–0.05 µM, Fig. 2E) with no explicit confidence interval or bootstrap resampling reported; the fit quality and sensitivity to the choice of fitting range are not shown.

ATPase activity (Pi release rate: 0.030 ± 0.001 Pi/min/MreB, Fig. 1G) is measured at a single MreB concentration (0.5 mg/mL liposomes) with n=2 independent experiments; this is insufficient to establish the rate as a robust parameter, especially given the high precision claimed (SD of 0.001).

Statistical tests for comparisons between WT and mutant filament behaviors (e.g., Fig. 3D, 4B) are not explicitly named; the figure legends state "n = ..." but do not specify whether t-tests, Mann-Whitney U, or other tests were used, or whether assumptions (normality, equal variance) were checked.

questions: In the model (Fig. 4D, Supplementary 'Modeling MreB dynamics'), how sensitive are the predictions in Fig. 4C and Fig. S10 to the choice of rate constants, particularly kₕᵧ𝒹 and k₋,𝒅? A one-way sensitivity analysis would clarify which parameters most strongly drive the predicted disassembly kinetics.

Figure 3I shows D158A filaments incorporate ATP* ~2× faster than WT (slopes 28.8 vs 12.2 intensity/min). Is this difference statistically significant, and does it reflect a genuine difference in nucleotide exchange kinetics or a consequence of D158A's lower ATP affinity (Fig. 3B) leading to more frequent binding attempts?

The authors state that MreB monomers are "partially unfolded in the absence of nucleotide" (line 107), explaining slow ATP/ADP binding kinetics. Is this claim supported by circular dichroism, hydrogen-deuterium exchange, or other structural data, or is it an inference from the kinetic data alone?

weaknesses.text: The manuscript claims nucleotide exchange within filaments is novel to MreB, yet ParM (ref. 29, Garner et al. 2004)—another prokaryotic actin homolog—appears to exhibit nucleotide exchange at filament ends (line 283); the manuscript does not clearly establish whether ParM's end-exchange mechanism is fundamentally different from MreB's intrafilament exchange, or whether the novelty claim should be narrowed to "intrafilament (not just end) exchange."

The authors argue that ATP hydrolysis is not required for polymerization, supported by E136A and D158A mutants, and cite ref. 29 (Garner et al. 2004) for the equivalent E136A mutation in ParM abolishing ATPase activity; however, the manuscript does not cite or discuss whether Garner et al. tested whether ParM E136A polymerizes, which would establish a precedent for uncoupling hydrolysis from polymerization in prokaryotic actins.

The manuscript proposes that intrafilament nucleotide exchange defines a new class of self-organizing filament dynamics but does not discuss whether the membrane context is essential to this mechanism or merely facilitates it; it is unclear whether the exchange mechanism would occur in solution-phase MreB filaments or is strictly a membrane-templated phenomenon.

The claim that MreB nucleotide binding rates are "~300-fold lower than those reported for actin" (line 96) cites Table 1, which compares to actin values from refs. 40–41; these actin values should be verified to be from the same experimental conditions (Mg²⁺ concentration, temperature, pH) to ensure the comparison is fair.

The manuscript attributes the proposal that "Pi release promotes depolymerization" in Geobacillus MreB to ref. 10 (Mao et al. 2023), but does not cite whether Mao et al. themselves proposed this or were reporting an earlier hypothesis; the attribution chain should be verified as primary.

Line 268 states "nucleotide exchange within MreB filaments" is "to our knowledge, this is the first report"—the ParM literature (ref. 29) should be explicitly checked for prior reports of any nucleotide exchange in prokaryotic actin filaments to confirm the claim's accuracy.

The in vivo CCCP experiment (Fig. 4J, lines 338–365) uses E136A as a proxy for ATP-bound filaments, but the manuscript does not discuss whether E136A's altered nucleotide binding affinity (Fig. 3B) might confound the interpretation; the experiment would be stronger if it also tested D158A or a true ATP-locked mutant.

Reference 17 (Adriaans et al., in press, 2026) is cited for nucleotide binding kinetics of Geobacillus MreB; this is a future publication and should be flagged as "in preparation" or "preprint" to signal its status to readers.

The manuscript cites Mao et al. (2023, ref. 10) as showing that "Escherichia coli MreB filaments recruit CL" (line 118), but Mao et al. studied Geobacillus MreB, not E. coli MreB; the attribution should be verified or clarified for species.

The critical concentration estimate (Cc ≈ 0.003 µM, line 179) is ~1000-fold lower than prior estimates of 1–2 µM (refs. 14–17), but the manuscript does not discuss why; a brief explanation of whether this reflects differences in assay conditions (membrane vs. solution) would strengthen the claim.

The model (Fig. 4D, Supplementary) includes a parameter for intrafilament nucleotide exchange rate (k₊,ₙ = 0.28 µM⁻¹·s⁻¹), but the manuscript does not cite or justify this value; it should state whether it is fitted to the FRAP data or derived from literature.

questions: Does the ParM literature (Garner et al. 2004, ref. 29) report whether ParM E136A polymerizes, and if so, does it establish that ATP hydrolysis is uncoupled from polymerization in prokaryotic actins prior to this work?
Is the nucleotide exchange mechanism in MreB strictly membrane-dependent, or would it occur in solution-phase filaments if they could form?
Reference 17 (Adriaans et al. 2026): is this a preprint, in-press, or in-preparation manuscript, and should its status be clarified in the reference list?

weaknesses.text: The claim that 'nucleotide exchange within filaments tunes their stability' rests primarily on FRAP recovery of ATP* (Fig. 3F) and the observation that WT filaments depolymerize faster in ADP than in buffer alone (Fig. 4A-B). However, the design does not exclude an alternative: ADP could destabilize filaments by direct binding to subunits without requiring exchange—i.e., ADP-bound subunits may simply dissociate faster than ATP-bound ones, regardless of whether nucleotide cycling occurs. The ATP* FRAP recovery shows nucleotide can exchange, but does not prove that exchange is the mechanism by which ADP destabilizes filaments. To distinguish these, the authors would need to measure the nucleotide state of filaments during depolymerization (e.g., by directly quantifying ADP incorporation into filaments during the ADP-flush experiment) or show that blocking exchange (if possible) prevents ADP-induced destabilization. The current evidence is consistent with exchange but does not prove it is the operative mechanism.

The quantification of intrafilament nucleotide exchange rates relies on ATP* FRAP recovery (Fig. 3F, 3I) and the kinetics of ATP* incorporation into preformed filaments (Fig. 3H-I). However, ATP* is a non-hydrolysable analogue with lower polymerization efficiency than ATP (Fig. S5), and the fluorophore may alter binding kinetics or accessibility. The authors show ATP* binds competitively (Fig. S2C), but do not directly measure whether ATP* exchange kinetics match those of native ATP. The Monte Carlo model uses exchange rates inferred from these ATP* experiments, so if ATP* kinetics differ substantially from ATP, the model's predictions about WT filament behavior under physiological nucleotide pools may not hold. Measuring exchange with native ATP (e.g., by pulse-chase with radioactive ATP) would strengthen this claim.

The in vivo experiment (Fig. 4J) shows that E136A filaments remain stable when ATP is depleted by CCCP, consistent with the model, but the design does not rule out that E136A's stability results from altered membrane binding or protein-protein interactions rather than ATP hydrolysis per se. The mutant has higher ATP affinity (Fig. 3B), which could independently stabilize filaments on the membrane. A more direct test would be to measure whether E136A filaments remain stable in the presence of ADP (which should destabilize WT filaments) in vivo, isolating the effect of nucleotide state from other properties of the mutant.

questions: Figure 3F (FRAP of ATP*-labeled filaments): what is the mobile fraction and half-recovery time, and how do these compare quantitatively to the ATP* incorporation rates measured in Fig. 3H-I to confirm they reflect the same exchange process?

In the Monte Carlo model, how sensitive are the predictions in Fig. 4I (filament stability under different nucleotide pools) to the inferred exchange rate constant k_{+,n} and k_{-,n}? Does a 2-fold or 5-fold change in these rates alter the qualitative predictions?

The ADP-flush experiment (Fig. 4A-B) shows rapid depolymerization, but does the filament length decrease linearly or accelerate over time, and does this match the model's prediction of a transition from k_{-,t} to k_{-,d} as ATP is depleted?

In Fig. 3H, why are D158A filaments not visible under standard ATP* labeling (17:1 ATP:ATP*) but become visible when exposed to pure ATP*? Does this indicate that D158A has lower affinity for ATP* specifically, or that the low ATP affinity of D158A prevents filament formation under the mixed nucleotide condition?

weaknesses.text: The claim that this is the "first report of nucleotide cycling within a biological polymer" is overstated. The manuscript cites ParM filaments where free ADP increases disassembly rate "proposed to result from nucleotide exchange at filament ends" (line 313, ref. 29). While the authors distinguish their finding as intrafilament rather than end-localized, nucleotide exchange in actin-like filaments is not unprecedented; the novelty is the mechanism and rate of intrafilament exchange in MreB, not the phenomenon itself.

The FRAP evidence for nucleotide exchange (Fig. 3F, ATP* recovery) does not exclude the alternative that ATP* recovery reflects preferential loss and rebinding of ATP*-labeled subunits at filament ends rather than exchange within intact subunits. The authors attribute lack of TFLime recovery (Fig. 3E) to photochemical trapping rather than nucleotide immobility, but this interpretation is plausible but not independently verified.

The claim that ATP hydrolysis occurs within filaments (rather than at ends) is inferred from slow Pi release and filament stability, not directly measured. The model fits the data but does not prove the location of hydrolysis; direct measurement of Pi release from preformed filaments blocked from polymerizing would be needed.

The relationship to concurrent work (de San Eustaquio-Campillo et al., 2026, PPR, cited as "in preparation" for G. stearothermophilus MreB mutants) should be clarified to establish priority and avoid duplication.

The explanation for the plateau in elongation rate (Fig. 2E)—attributed to 2D diffusion on the membrane—is qualitative; lateral diffusion coefficients for membrane-bound MreB are not measured, leaving the explanation unverified.
The model contains many fitted parameters (Table 1); sensitivity analysis or parameter uncertainty is not discussed, limiting confidence in quantitative predictions.
The in vivo CCCP experiment (Fig. 4J) shows delocalization of WT MreB but does not characterize the timescale or distinguish between disassembly, depolymerization, and loss of membrane binding.
The comparison of nucleotide exchange rate to Pi release rate (line 330) uses parameters with different units and is not made explicit in the text, making the claim difficult to verify.

questions: Does ATP* recovery in the FRAP experiment (Fig. 3F) occur in E136A filaments, which do not exchange nucleotides (Fig. 3H)? If not, this would directly support the exchange mechanism and exclude end-dynamics alternatives.
What is the lateral diffusion coefficient of membrane-bound MreB, and does it match the 2D-diffusion explanation for the plateau in elongation rate (Fig. 2E)?

Can Pi release be measured from preformed filaments in the absence of polymerization (e.g., by blocking monomer addition with a high-affinity cap) to directly test whether hydrolysis occurs within filaments or at ends?
How does the timescale of MreB delocalization upon CCCP treatment (Fig. 4J) compare to the predicted filament disassembly rate, and is delocalization reversible upon ATP restoration?
What is the relationship and priority between this manuscript and the concurrent work by de San Eustaquio-Campillo et al. (2026, PPR) on MreB polymerization cycles?

weaknesses.text: **Load-bearing claim: Intrafilament nucleotide exchange occurs in MreB filaments.** The evidence rests on FRAP experiments (Fig. 3F, 3H) showing rapid recovery of ATP* signal in preformed filaments, interpreted as nucleotide exchange. However, the manuscript does not exclude the alternative that ATP* fluorescence recovery reflects rebinding of ATP* monomers from solution to filament ends or to transiently dissociated subunits, rather than exchange within the intact filament lattice. The authors state "Although TFLime binding to pFAST is reversible under normal imaging conditions, the lack of FRAP recovery suggests that the high-intensity laser illumination used for photobleaching induces irreversible photochemical trapping" (line 254–256), but this explanation applies only to the TFLime experiment (Fig. 3E), not to ATP* (Fig. 3F). For ATP*, the recovery could arise from 2D diffusion of ATP*-MreB monomers on the membrane surface and rebinding at filament ends, a mechanism the authors acknowledge for polymerization (lines 189–191) but do not rule out for the FRAP recovery. The capping experiment (Fig. 4G–H) shows that ADP-induced depolymerization occurs in the WT section of a filament capped with E136A, consistent with intrafilament nucleotide exchange, but the fragmentation observed could also result from nucleotide-dependent conformational changes that destabilize the filament without requiring nucleotide exchange within the lattice. To distinguish intrafilament exchange from end-mediated rebinding, the authors would need to show that recovery occurs at positions far from filament ends, or that recovery rate is independent of filament length or end density.

**Load-bearing claim: The Monte-Carlo model accurately reproduces experimental observations and supports the mechanistic interpretation.** The model is described only in prose and supplementary text (referenced as 'Supplementary Information, Modeling MreB dynamics', line 286), with no equations, pseudocode, or parameter-fitting procedure provided in the main text or accessible supplementary materials. The authors state standard values (Fig. 4D) but do not specify: (i) how these values were derived (fitted to which data, using which algorithm, with what objective function?); (ii) sensitivity analysis or confidence intervals for fitted parameters; (iii) the exact sequence of reactions and their rate laws; (iv) initial conditions and boundary conditions for simulations; (v) the number of stochastic replicates and convergence criteria. Without this detail, the model cannot be reimplemented or validated independently. The agreement between simulations (Fig. S10) and experiments (Fig. 4A–C) is qualitative; no quantitative goodness-of-fit metric is reported. The model's predictive power is therefore unverifiable.

**Load-bearing claim: ATP hydrolysis is not required for MreB polymerization.** The evidence is that E136A and D158A mutants, which have reduced ATPase activity (Fig. 3A), still polymerize with kinetics similar to WT (Fig. 3C–D). However, the manuscript does not report the absolute ATPase activity of these mutants—only that Pi release is 'markedly reduced' (line 232). If the mutants retain even 5–10% of WT ATPase activity, hydrolysis could still be mechanistically required for polymerization but kinetically slow enough that it does not limit the observed elongation rate. The authors should quantify the residual ATPase activity of E136A and D158A in absolute terms (Pi/min/MreB) and show that it is negligible compared to the polymerization rate.

Image-processing parameters for TSOAX filament tracking (line 808) are not specified: no threshold values, window sizes, or sensitivity settings are given, making the elongation-rate measurements (Fig. 2E) non-reproducible.

The FRAP analysis (Fig. 3E–F) does not report the bleach radius, recovery half-time, or lateral diffusion coefficient, preventing verification of the claim that 'monomers do not turnover within filaments' (line 254).

The photobleaching experiment (Fig. 2G) uses a 'growth-ratio definition' (line 221) that is relegated to the figure legend without explicit statement of the formula or how stochastic fluctuations were distinguished from intrinsic polarity.

Raw data (HS-AFM images, TIRF time-lapses, fluorescence anisotropy traces, ATPase assay replicates) are stated to be 'available from the corresponding authors upon request' (line 883) rather than deposited with a DOI or accession number, violating the In Silico standard for load-bearing empirical data.
Code for the Monte-Carlo model is not mentioned as available anywhere; the supplementary text reference (line 286) is not a resolvable artifact.

questions: What is the absolute Pi release rate (Pi/min/MreB) for E136A and D158A mutants, and how does it compare to the polymerization rate (subunits/min) to establish whether hydrolysis is truly dispensable?

For the ATP* FRAP experiment (Fig. 3F), what is the bleach radius, recovery half-time, and fitted lateral diffusion coefficient, and how does the recovery curve distinguish intrafilament exchange from end-mediated rebinding?
What are the TSOAX parameter values (threshold, window size, sensitivity) used for filament tracking, and are these parameters consistent across all experiments?

Can the authors provide the complete Monte-Carlo model (reactions, rate laws, initial/boundary conditions, fitting procedure, parameter uncertainties) as a supplementary text or deposited code repository with a DOI?
Where will raw data (HS-AFM stacks, TIRF movies, fluorescence anisotropy traces, ATPase replicates) be deposited, and what is the accession number or DOI?

weaknesses.text: **Mechanism of nucleotide exchange is inferred, not demonstrated.** The authors propose that membrane anchoring reduces twist angle and opens the nucleotide-binding pocket to permit exchange (lines 268–283), but this is a conformational hypothesis unsupported by structural data or direct conformational measurements. The evidence shows that exchange *occurs* and that it depends on ATPase activity (E136A shows no recovery in Fig. 3F), but not *why* the pocket opens. The alternative—that the membrane-bound state simply has inherently higher nucleotide off-rates regardless of pocket geometry—is not excluded. This is SOFT overclaiming of mechanism: the claim 'membrane anchoring was not or only poorly considered in these studies' (line 269) is true, but the authors then assert a specific conformational model without testing it. Resolve by: (1) stating the mechanism as 'consistent with' rather than asserting it, or (2) measuring nucleotide dissociation rates from membrane-bound vs. soluble MreB directly, or (3) performing molecular dynamics on membrane-anchored MreB to test the twist-angle hypothesis.

**Generalization to B. subtilis in vivo is supported only by one indirect experiment.** The CCCP delocalization experiment (Fig. 4J, lines 338–357) shows that E136A-MreB remains membrane-localized when ATP is depleted, consistent with the model. However, this is a single condition in a single strain, and the authors do not measure nucleotide composition in vivo, ATP/ADP ratios, or whether the predicted nucleotide exchange actually occurs in living cells. The claim 'in growing cells, high ATP levels maintain MreB filaments on the membrane through intrafilament nucleotide exchange' (lines 350–351) is supported by the CCCP result but not by direct evidence of exchange occurring in vivo. The in vivo section reads as extrapolation from in vitro findings rather than direct validation. Resolve by: measuring intracellular ATP/ADP ratios and correlating them with MreB stability, or using fluorescent nucleotide analogs in live cells to detect exchange.

**Nucleotide binding kinetics are anomalously slow and poorly explained.** The ATP and ADP binding rates to soluble MreB are ~300-fold slower than actin (line 100), and the authors propose that MreB is 'partially unfolded in the absence of nucleotide' and requires conformational rearrangement (lines 101–103). This explanation is plausible but not tested: no evidence of unfolding is presented (no circular dichroism, thermal stability, or hydrodynamic measurements). The A260/A280 ratio (0.62) indicates little bound nucleotide but does not address protein folding. This matters because the slow binding kinetics are unusual and central to understanding MreB assembly dynamics. Resolve by: measuring the hydrodynamic radius or secondary structure of nucleotide-free MreB, or performing stopped-flow kinetics to test whether a conformational step limits binding.

The claim that nucleotide exchange 'tunes filament stability' (abstract, line 42) is supported for the WT case but the D158A mutant shows that low nucleotide affinity (not exchange per se) drives rapid disassembly, leaving unclear whether exchange itself is the tuning mechanism or merely a consequence of the nucleotide-binding properties.

Figure 3H shows homogeneous ATP* binding along WT and D158A filaments but not E136A; the authors interpret this as evidence that E136A cannot exchange nucleotides, but the figure also shows E136A filaments are not visible under standard labeling conditions (line 261), making the comparison indirect.

The model assumes 'identical dynamics at both filament-ends' (Fig. 4D legend), but the photobleaching experiment (Fig. 2G) shows occasional asymmetry in elongation rates; the impact of this assumption on predictions is not discussed.

The critical concentration derived from TIRF (0.003 µM, line 177) is much lower than the 1–2 µM used in most experiments; the authors do not discuss whether the plateau in elongation rate (Fig. 2E) reflects a real biological saturation or an artifact of the labeling strategy at higher concentrations.

questions: What is the nucleotide dissociation rate from membrane-bound MreB subunits, and does it differ from soluble MreB?
Can you measure the nucleotide composition of MreB filaments in living B. subtilis cells, and does it match the predicted ATP/ADP ratio from the model?
Does the secondary structure or hydrodynamic radius of nucleotide-free MreB differ from ATP-bound MreB, supporting the proposed unfolding hypothesis?
